messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 22
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: School Principal
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 71

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Old Memories: Old photos, Unpredictability: Unpredictable situations, Dream Residue: Waking up from a nightmare
  Memory: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
  Negative Appraisals: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kwame is twenty-two years old and the principal of a small private school in a Midwestern city, a position he earned through sheer determination and an unnerving competence that had always set him apart from other young men his age. But in the quiet hours before dawn, after waking from a nightmare that leaves him drenched in sweat, he does not feel competent. He feels fragmented, as if the pieces of his life do not quite fit together, and he cannot recall exactly what the nightmare was about — only the residue: a thick, choking dread that lingers in his chest long after he has checked the locks on his apartment door for the third time.

The nightmare always returns to the same place, though he cannot deliberately call up the memory. When he tries to remember what happened to him as a child, the details slip away like smoke. He knows only that his father — his primary caregiver after his mother left — had a terrible temper, and that the beatings were not daily but entirely unpredictable. That unpredictability is what Kwame fears most now. A sudden shift in a student’s tone, a door slamming in the hallway, the unexpected cancellation of a scheduled staff meeting — these moments send a spike of alertness through him that he cannot explain to anyone. He has come to believe that he has permanently changed for the worse because of those years, that something inside him was broken and never healed right.

The memories that do surface often come in fragments: the sting of a leather belt across his back, the sound of his father’s voice rising without warning, the sensation of his own small body pressing itself into a corner. These fragments feel more real than anything else in his day. When he looks at old photographs — a pile of them his aunt sent him last month that he has not opened — he cannot bear to touch them. He knows the photos are harmless paper, but his body reacts before his mind can catch up: his hands tremble, his throat tightens, and he shoves the envelope into the back of a closet. At work, he avoids the school’s annual photo archive, telling the secretary he is too busy to help with the yearbook. He is not too busy; he is afraid that a single image from his own childhood will pull him under.

Kwame has been with his girlfriend, Amara, for two years, and she has noticed that he never talks about his past. She does not push, but she has also noticed how tightly he holds himself together. When they argue — small things, like whose turn it is to do the dishes — he goes silent and still, and she mistakes his stillness for coldness. In truth, Kwame is terrified that if he lets the anger rise, he will not be able to stop it. He has a vivid, horrifying image of himself becoming his father, of doing something terrible to someone he loves. So he suppresses every flash of irritation until it hardens into a knot in his stomach. At school, the same fear makes him an unusually calm principal — praised for his patience — but that patience costs him. He lies awake some nights, replaying a tense conversation with a parent, certain that he was only one wrong word away from losing control.

The helplessness he feels is pervasive. He cannot stop bad things from happening — not to himself, not to his students, not to anyone. When a first-grader fell and scraped her knee on the playground last week, Kwame’s first thought was not to comfort her but to scan the yard for the next threat. He stood frozen for a moment, his heart pounding, before the school nurse rushed past him. Afterward, he sat in his office and stared at the wall, convinced that he was fundamentally unfit for a job that required him to protect children. He had not protected himself as a child; why would he be able to protect anyone else?

What finally brought Kwame to seek help was a series of mornings like this one: waking from a nightmare with the feeling that he was still someone else’s punching bag, and then going to work and smiling at the children, all the while monitoring every unpredictable shift in the air around him — a sudden silence from a classroom, an unexpected knock on his door, a change of schedule written on the whiteboard. He came to therapy because Amara told him, gently, that she could not keep watching him live in a state of hidden terror. He came because he is exhausted. And he came because, despite everything, he hopes that the pieces might someday fit together into a whole person — and that he might be able to remember his own story without it feeling more real than his life now.
